contentBlocks.text: Welcome to Grade 11 ELA. This year builds toward college-level research and writing — and every strong research project starts with one thing: a genuinely good question.

A strong research question is focused (narrow enough to actually answer in the space you have), open (not answerable with a simple yes/no or single fact), and genuinely researchable (real sources exist to investigate it). Compare: 'What is climate change?' (too broad — an entire field, not a question), 'Did it rain in Seattle in 2020?' (too narrow — a single fact, not real research), versus 'How have Pacific Northwest cities adapted their infrastructure in response to changing rainfall patterns?' (focused, open, and researchable). Take a broad topic you're genuinely curious about and narrow it into one focused, open, researchable question.

A strong research question shapes everything that follows — the sources you'll look for, the argument you'll build, even how you'll organize your final paper. Tomorrow we'll look at how to evaluate whether a source is actually trustworthy enough to use.

objectives: Identify the three qualities of a strong research question: focused, open, researchable
Narrow a broad topic into one focused, open, researchable question
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Introduce the three qualities of a strong research question with the climate-change/Seattle-rain/PNW-infrastructure examples.
2. Discuss why 'too broad' and 'too narrow' both fail, just in different ways.
3. Have the child pick a genuine topic of interest and narrow it into a research question.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's topic: evaluating source credibility.
differentiationTips: Struggling: provide 3-4 broad topics (space exploration, video games, a sport) to choose from rather than requiring the child to generate one from nothing
Ready for more: ask them to write two DIFFERENT focused questions from the same broad topic, exploring different angles
This is the first lesson of the year — a good moment to frame the whole unit as building toward a real research paper, not isolated skill drills
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. The three qualities are focused, open, and researchable. 2. A question that's too broad ('What is X?') can't be meaningfully answered in a limited paper; one that's too narrow (a single yes/no fact) doesn't require real research. 3. A strong question narrows a broad topic to something specific enough to investigate but open enough to require real analysis.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Writing standard W.11-12.7: conducting short and sustained research projects to answer a self-generated question, narrowing or broadening the inquiry as needed.
